C0.quote: each district elects multiple representatives, potentially through a non-winner-take-all voting rule
C0.note: Studies multi-winner voting rules (Thiele, STV) combined with redistricting; empirical/computational.

C1.quote: We carry out large-scale empirical analyses for the U.S. House of Representatives
C1.note: Main results are empirical analyses on real election data, gerrymandering map optimisation, simulation of voter rankings in Section 4. Proposition 1 is a small analytic result. Proportionality is an evaluation criterion; the WD tag is a judgement call.

C2.1.value: set of approved candidates or a ranking over candidates
C2.1.quote: either a set of approved candidates or a ranking over candidates

C2.2.quote: either a set of approved candidates or a ranking over candidates
C2.2.note: Thiele rules use approval sets; STV uses complete rankings.

C2.3.quote: The utility that voter v assigns to candidate c is
C2.3.note: Voter utilities and party membership/partisan scores are used in the simulation.

C2.4.quote: each voter simply approves all the candidates in their party
C2.4.note: Votes are derived directly from party and partisan scores/utilities. No statement about submission versus held attitude or about truthfulness.

C3.1.quote: unlike in actual elections, we assume that there is no ballot exhaustion
C3.1.note: All voters are non-strategic: they approve their party's candidates or rank by utility with noise. Only the map drawer is strategic.

C3.2.note: Voters' behaviour is assumed (party-line approval, ranking by utility plus noise) but there is no statement that submitted ballots equal held attitudes.

C4.1.note: Rankings are generated by ordering candidates by a spatial random utility. Voters' welfare is not otherwise used, but this is the only utility-input link.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used.

C5.1.quote: we primarily consider proportionality: how does the fraction of winners
C5.1.note: Proportionality of party seat share to vote share, evaluated as representation of voters and groups; competitiveness is also evaluated.

C5.2.quote: the fraction of winners wp belonging to each party p
C5.2.note: Seat share is compared with vote share (party membership), derived from the party-line input assumptions. No statement relates it to held attitudes.

VOT.quote_behav: each voter simply approves all the candidates in their party
VOT.note: Voters follow solid coalitions or random-utility rankings.

CAN.note: Candidates are generated synthetically and take no action.

ORG.note: Nobody in the model acts as chair or election authority.

DIS.quote_behav: a party can gerrymander a map to maximize the seats won by their party
DIS.quote_info: the optimizer observes the voter ranking realizations over candidates when drawing maps
DIS.note: Partisan map drawers optimise; independent commissions optimise fairness. Information is the historical vote shares as the baseline, with the foreseeable-noise variant as a robustness check, so it is arguably PARTIAL. COMPLETE is chosen for the perfect-knowledge variant.

DES.note: The design recommendations are not formally modelled as a designer's objective.

C7.1.quote: Note that the various components of the election procedure may be determined by different actors
C7.1.note: The district designer is STRAT; voters are NONSTRAT.

C7.2.note: The paper justifies solid coalitions as an empirical simplification but gives no argument for why voters are non-strategic while the map drawer is strategic.

C8.1.quote: the most gerrymandered map for each party
C8.1.note: Map optimisation by dynamic or integer program is an optimisation problem of the districting agent.

claims.quote: fairness-minded independent commissions would be able to achieve proportional outcomes in every state
using a winner-take-all procedure with MMDs ... should be avoided
this part of the proposal could be relaxed without sacrificing its proportionality goals

C9.1.note: The claims concern real institutions, the Fair Representation Act, and rule choice.

C9.2.quote: our results should not be interpreted as what would necessarily happen
C9.2.note: The claims need the assumptions that voters vote party-line or by spatial utility, i.e. sincere voting with no strategic behaviour, and that input equals held attitude. The solid coalitions and spatial assumptions are stated, but sincerity and the input-attitude relation are not.

C10.1.note: The paper does not state a procedural reading.
